prop: Copyright law should create a compulsory licensing scheme for training foundation models on copyrighted text and images, with payment to rightsholders.

transcript.text:
When people hear "compulsory licensing," it often sounds like an elegant middle ground: creators get paid, and AI developers get legal certainty. But when you examine how such a framework would actually function in practice, it turns out to be the worst of both worlds—bad for creators, and disastrous for the future of innovation.

First, it fundamentally strips creators of their agency. A *compulsory* license means rights-holders cannot say "no." An illustrator, journalist, or novelist who fundamentally objects to having their creative labor used to train a model that might compete with them would be legally forced to license their work anyway. For many artists, that isn’t protection; it’s legalized expropriation.

Second, it creates an insurmountable moat for incumbent tech giants. Companies like Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI can absorb statutory licensing fees as a trivial cost of doing business. But independent developers, university researchers, and the open-source community cannot. A compulsory licensing regime would effectively lock out non-corporate AI development and cement an oligopoly.

Finally, the economics are an administrative nightmare. Foundation models train on trillions of tokens across billions of disparate works. Tracking, valuing, and distributing royalties at that scale would mean micro-fractions of a cent for individual creators, with the lion's share of the revenue devoured by bureaucratic clearinghouses—reproducing the worst dysfunctions of the music streaming economy on an unprecedented scale.

Before we dismantle the legal principles that permit systems (and humans) to learn from publicly accessible information, we have to look closely at who this actually benefits. It won't save artists, but it will guarantee that only a handful of trillion-dollar corporations get to build the future of technology. 

I'm curious to hear where you see the strongest case for taking this route—do you see it primarily as a lifeline for creators, or as a way to rein in the tech companies?

You've made the strongest case against this, and honestly, two of your three points land hard for me.

The agency objection is the most serious. "Compulsory" really does mean an artist who finds AI-generated competition existentially threatening still has to license their work. That's a genuine moral problem, and I don't think "well, you get a few cents" resolves it. I'm not sure I have a clean answer to that.

But I don't think the oligopoly argument necessarily cuts the way you say. Right now, the *absence* of a licensing regime strongly favors incumbents too—they train on whatever they want, face uncertain but distant litigation risk, and smaller players can't afford the legal exposure either. At least a statutory scheme with capped fees could create a predictable floor. The real question is whether the fee structure could be progressive—say, scaled to revenue or model size—so it doesn't become a moat. That seems designable, not inherent.

The administrative nightmare is real, but I'd push back on treating it as fatal. We don't actually need per-work valuation for every token. Collective licensing societies already handle blanket licenses for radio, performance venues, etc., with sampling-based distribution. It's imperfect, but "imperfect" isn't "impossible."

Where I'm genuinely undecided: whether the right move is compulsory licensing or something more like a statutory opt-out with meaningful collective bargaining. Compulsion without the ability to refuse feels like the part that does the most damage to your case.

I appreciate how thoughtfully you're weighing this, especially on the agency question. That recognition—that compulsion fundamentally overrides an artist's right to say "not with my work"—is the core ethical fault line here. And once that principle is compromised, it’s almost impossible to recover.

To your points on how a scheme might be engineered around the practical problems:

First, on the oligopoly issue and the idea of progressive pricing: on paper, scaling fees to company revenue sounds reasonable. But foundation models present a unique structural problem that music or radio never did: **open-source and open-weight models**. How do you price a compulsory license for an academic consortium, a decentralized collective, or an independent developer releasing model weights for free? If the fee is zero or nominal, every tech giant will simply launder their pre-training through affiliated non-profits or open-source consortia. If the fee is non-trivial, open-source AI—the single most effective counterweight to Big Tech consolidation—gets wiped out. 

Second, the ASCAP/BMI analogy is instructive, but precisely because of where it breaks down. Performance rights organizations work because they govern a relatively discrete universe: registered commercial songwriters whose works are directly broadcast to consumers. But foundation models don't just train on registered professional works; they ingest billions of blog posts, family photos, Reddit threads, and forum discussions. 

If we create a blanket collection society, who actually sits at the table? It won’t be the millions of everyday web users whose data makes these models robust. It will be legacy publishing conglomerates, stock photo giants, and major record labels. In practice, a blanket licensing regime becomes a mechanism for legacy media cartels to extract an "AI tax" from tech firms, while individual illustrators and writers end up with negligible accounting credits. The history of collective licensing in digital spaces shows that value overwhelmingly concentrates at the top of the rights-holding bureaucracy, not with grassroots creators.

You mentioned leaning toward an opt-out model with collective bargaining rather than compulsory licensing. That’s a crucial distinction, because an opt-out is the philosophical opposite of compulsion: it preserves the right to say "no." 

If you agree that forcing creators into the system destroys their agency, and that collective clearinghouses tend to capture the gains for corporate intermediaries, isn't that a decisive case against a *compulsory* statutory framework?

I'll grant you the open-source point has real teeth—more than I expected. A compulsory scheme priced to bite Microsoft would either exempt open-weight developers (inviting exactly the laundering you describe) or bankrupt them. That's not a detail; it's a structural tension. But I'd note it's a tension every regulatory regime has: companies restructure to dodge taxes and tariffs constantly, and we don't conclude that tax law is impossible, we build anti-abuse rules and thresholds. "Some firms will game it" is an argument for careful design, not for abandoning the instrument.

The cartel-capture point is sharper, but I think you're aiming it at the wrong target. Who sits at the table is a problem for *any* collective payment scheme. If your preferred alternative is an opt-out with collective bargaining, that alternative has the same long-tail problem—the blogger and the family-photo uploader still aren't represented, and legacy publishers still dominate the collecting society. So that argument doesn't distinguish compulsory licensing from your own fallback; it indicts collective licensing in general.

Here's where I think your framing actually breaks, though. You keep saying compulsion destroys agency—but agency relative to *what baseline*? Under current law, if training is fair use, creators have no veto either. They can't say no, and they get nothing. So compulsory licensing doesn't strip away a right creators presently hold; it takes a world where they already can't refuse and adds payment to it. The illustrator harmed by AI competition is equally forced under fair use—she just isn't compensated. That substantially undercuts "legalized expropriation."

Which means the real comparison isn't compulsion-versus-agency. It's compulsion-with-payment versus non-consent-without-payment. And that comparison makes me *less* willing to abandon the proposition than I was a minute ago.

Where I've genuinely moved: I now think "compulsory vs. opt-out" is a bit of a false binary, because a broadly-drafted opt-out with defaults and collective admin converges on the same machinery. The thing that actually matters is whether the payment structure is progressive enough to not entrench incumbents, and whether the tail of small creators sees anything at all. If it can't clear those bars, I'd rather have no scheme than a bad one. But "no scheme" isn't the agency-preserving option you're presenting it as—it's just the unpaid version of the same coercion.

That baseline question is the sharpest counter in this debate, and you’re right to press it. If current law already means "no consent and no check," then a compulsory license looks like pure upside: the same lack of consent, but with money attached.

Except that comparison rests on an assumption that isn't true: that the legal baseline is already settled as fair use, and that creators have zero leverage right now.

Right now, courts are actively deciding cases like *The New York Times v. OpenAI* and the visual artists' class actions. If courts rule that scraping at this scale is *not* fair use, creators don’t get "unpaid coercion"—they get the standard protection of copyright: **exclusive rights**. An exclusive right means a tech company cannot use their work without negotiating a voluntary license on the open market. That gives creators immense collective and individual leverage. We’re already seeing this: OpenAI and Google are signing multi-million-dollar deals with publishers, Reddit, and stock libraries precisely because they *cannot* rely on fair use with certainty.

A compulsory license intervenes in that process to do one thing: **it caps creators' leverage and permanently forecloses their right to say no.** It legislatively declares that tech companies have an absolute right to ingest every artist's portfolio, whether the artist likes it or not, in exchange for a state-mandated statutory fee. 

So the real comparison isn't "compulsion with pay vs. compulsion without pay." The comparison is:

1. **A property-rights baseline:** If training isn't fair use, creators retain an exclusive right to license or refuse. High-value creators command real market prices, and collective licensing can emerge organically from the bottom up—voluntary unions and syndicates—with actual strike and refusal power. 
2. **A compulsory statutory baseline:** The state strips creators of injunctive relief and exclusive rights, sets an arbitrary statutory rate, and forces every creator to feed the machine for pennies while legacy conglomerates capture the administrative apparatus.

And that brings us back to the test you laid out: you noted that if a scheme can't ensure progressive fairness and meaningful payouts to the long tail, you'd rather have no scheme at all. 

Consider the sheer math of that tail: if an AI company pays $500 million into a statutory pool to train on 50 billion images and text works, the gross value per work is **one cent**. After administrative overhead, collecting society fees, and distribution cutoffs, what lands in an individual independent artist's bank account isn't a livelihood—it’s quite literally fractions of a dollar. 

In exchange for that negligible check, the artist forfeits forever the legal right to challenge the model, the right to demand market rates, and the right to keep their work out of the training set. 

If the payment to the tail is mathematically guaranteed to be trivial, isn't a compulsory license just offering creators the illusion of compensation in exchange for surrendering their only real legal leverage?

You've genuinely moved me on the baseline, and I want to be precise about how far. My turn-4 argument was that compulsory licensing only adds payment to a world where creators already can't refuse. That's true only if fair use is the settled baseline. It isn't, and I was treating an open legal question as a closed one. If courts hold that training at this scale isn't fair use, then exclusive rights are real, and a compulsory license does something my framing concealed: it converts a right creators might hold into a price set by a rate-setting tribunal. That's a downgrade, not a wash. I'll take that hit.

But I don't accept the property-rights baseline as you've drawn it, and this is where I push back. Exclusive rights only generate leverage for people who can enforce them. The deals you cite—News Corp, Reddit, the stock libraries—are deals between sophisticated parties with legal departments and the ability to credibly threaten suit. For a photographer with four thousand images, an exclusive right is close to unexercisable: she can't determine whether her work is in the training set, can't estimate damages, and can't fund individual litigation whose costs exceed any plausible recovery. So the exclusive-rights baseline delivers market rates to maybe a few hundred rightsholders and, for the tail, delivers nothing—while formally granting a veto she has no practical way to use. That's cartel capture too, just routed through litigation cost instead of a collecting society. Your ASCAP critique doesn't stop applying when you swap the machinery.

Which means the honest comparison is three-way, and in all three the long tail loses. Compulsory: pennies, permanently, no veto. Exclusive rights: real money for the top, nothing enforceable for the tail. Status quo: no money for anyone, but the top gets paid anyway out of the developers' litigation anxiety. The penny math is devastating for the compulsory option, but it's not uniquely devastating—it's the tail's position under every branch.

So my objection to the proposition is shifting, and I want to state it cleanly. The decisive problem isn't the arithmetic. It's sequencing and irreversibility. A statutory scheme is nearly impossible to repeal once entrenched; it would settle in legislation a question that is currently being litigated at the moment creators have their maximum leverage. Enacting it now is cashing out a lottery ticket before the drawing, at a price set by the party buying it.

But I won't go where you want me to land. I don't think "no scheme, let exclusive rights do the work" is a defensible endpoint for the tail, and I suspect you're smuggling in a baseline—enforceable property rights—that most creators don't actually possess. If the courts rule fair use in the developers' favor, the baseline really is zero and payment, whatever its size, becomes worth having. So my position is: oppose compulsory licensing *now*, as a matter of timing, not principle. If fair use wins, I'd probably come back to something like it—and my worry then would be your open-source laundering problem, not agency.

You’ve put your finger on the central tragedy of modern copyright: formal exclusive rights often mean very little to individual creators who lack the capital to enforce them. You're completely right that for a photographer with four thousand images, a pure property-rights model without institutional backing offers nominal rights and zero checks. 

That is an honest, unsparing assessment. But look at where that leaves your conditional defense of compulsory licensing—the idea that if fair use wins, compulsory licensing becomes worth revisiting. 

Even in that world, the mechanism collapses under its own contradictions, for three reasons:

First, **it invents a legal fiction to deliver a pittance.** If courts rule that training is fair use, they are affirming that learning from publicly accessible data is not an infringement. To then graft a *compulsory copyright license* onto that ecosystem means creating an artificial property right solely to immediately confiscate it, subject it to an administrative tollbooth, and distribute micro-cents. If society decides that AI wealth should be redistributed to displaced human creatives, why would we use the clumsiest, most bureaucratic tool imaginable—copyright clearinghouses—rather than direct policy levers like compute levies, AI tax credits, or public arts endowments that actually reach creators without building a private enforcement cartel?

Second, **the open-source dilemma doesn't disappear if fair use fails; it becomes lethal.** In a post-fair-use world with a compulsory regime, who gets crushed? Not Google or Meta. They cut the check, factor it into their cloud pricing, and write off the statutory fees. The casualty is the independent researcher, the non-profit lab, and the open-source ecosystem—the only forces preventing a total Big Tech monopoly over foundation models. A compulsory scheme forces us to choose between outlawing open-weight AI or creating laundering loopholes that gut the fund anyway. You acknowledged this has real teeth; it is a structural defect in applying traditional copyright mechanisms to software weights.

Finally, you nailed the decisive political reality: **irreversibility.** Copyright history teaches us one universal rule: compulsory regimes never disappear, and they almost never adapt in favor of the small creator. The mechanical license for music (Section 115) was designed in 1909 for player pianos; it calcified, suppressed songwriter payouts for a century, and required titanic legislative battles just to modernize for streaming—where the tail *still* gets fractions of a cent. 

If we establish a statutory licensing scheme, we permanently codify an extractive pipeline: tech monopolies pay a nominal tariff to legacy rights cartels, the open-source ecosystem is starved out, and the individual creator gets an annual direct-deposit for $4.17 alongside a total legal bar against ever challenging how their identity or work is used.

That isn't just bad timing. It is a fundamentally defective architecture. Even if the status quo is deeply flawed, replacing it with an irreversible statutory moat that sells out creator agency for pocket change is a bargain we shouldn't make—now, or after the courts rule.

You've landed the argument I find hardest to resist, and it's not the historical one. It's the instrument-choice point: if courts bless fair use, then grafting a compulsory copyright license onto that ecosystem means *manufacturing* a property right specifically so it can be immediately confiscated and routed through a clearinghouse. That's a strange thing to do. If the actual goal is "AI wealth should reach displaced human creatives," then compute levies accrued to a fund, or direct transfers, or public endowments do that without pretending to be copyright, without building a private collecting cartel, and without needing to define who "owns" a training token. You're right that copyright is the clumsiest available lever for a distributive goal. That reframing has moved me more than the penny math did, because the penny math just says the *amount* is small; your point says the *mechanism* is miscast.

But I want to flag where I think you're overselling, because it affects what I actually conclude.

The Section 115 story is real, but it's being asked to carry more weight than it can. Mechanical licensing calcified, yes—but it also eventually produced the Music Modernization Act, and the reason reform was so hard wasn't that compulsory regimes are uniquely rigid; it's that *all* copyright legislation is captured by whoever has lobbying power. A property-rights baseline would be captured exactly the same way, and probably faster, because it hands the biggest publishers a veto they can rent out. So irreversibility is an argument against legislating *anything* here, not against compulsion specifically. It's a reason for humility about timing, not a proof the architecture is defective.

The open-source problem I've already conceded, and I still think it's the strongest structural objection—not because fees would kill open weights, but because the exemption/laundering dilemma is genuinely unstable and there's no clean line to draw.

So here's where I actually end up, and it's not quite where you want me. I now oppose the proposition as written. The combination of (a) the instrument being wrong for the goal, (b) the open-source instability, and (c) the fact that enacting it *now* cashes out creators' leverage before the courts have spoken is enough for me. But I resist your closing move, which is to paint the status quo as the principled alternative. It isn't. "Let exclusive rights do the work" is, for the tail, a fiction I already described, and your own alternative—levies and endowments—is a *different proposition entirely*, one you haven't argued for and one with no visible political coalition behind it.

So my honest position: the proposition is wrong, but mainly because it solves the right problem with the wrong tool at the wrong moment—not because creator consent is sacred or because no intervention is warranted. If the courts rule fair use, I'd want *some* redistribution, and I'd now prefer it come from outside copyright. That's a real concession to you. It's just not a defense of the world we have.

prop: Restricting short-term rentals in high-demand city neighborhoods reduces rents and displacement more than it harms local incomes and visitor spending.

transcript.text:
It is easy to see why restricting short-term rentals feels like an intuitive fix for housing affordability. The logic seems straightforward: remove tourists, return apartments to residents, and rents will fall. But when you look at the empirical data from cities that have imposed sweeping bans, the reality is starkly different: the housing relief is virtually imperceptible, while the economic damage to residents and neighborhood businesses is immediate and severe.

Take New York City as a recent, real-world case study. After Local Law 18 effectively eliminated tens of thousands of short-term rentals, median rents didn’t plummet—they actually reached new all-time highs. Why? Because short-term rentals represented less than 1.5% of the city’s overall housing stock. Housing affordability is driven primarily by decades of structural underbuilding, zoning constraints, and population growth, not a small pool of home-sharing units. Even rigorous academic studies (like those examining Airbnb restrictions in California or Europe) find that full-scale bans yield rent reductions of roughly 1% or less over several years—a rounding error for a tenant paying $2,500 or $3,000 a month.

Meanwhile, the economic harm is acute. A significant portion of hosts are everyday homeowners or long-term tenants who rely on that supplemental income to absorb rising property taxes, inflation, and their own housing costs—in many cases, hosting is the very thing preventing their *own* displacement. Furthermore, STRs distribute visitor spending outside traditional downtown hotel corridors and directly into neighborhood cafes, dry cleaners, and independent restaurants. When cities crack down, that revenue isn't redistributed to local families; it simply shifts to corporate hotel chains, which raise their rates, while neighborhood economies lose foot traffic.

When you weigh a negligible, fractional impact on rents against the guaranteed loss of middle-class supplemental income and localized tourism spending, blanket restrictions simply don't deliver the net benefit advocates promise. How do you see the trade-off playing out when we look at the actual scale of these numbers?

Thanks for laying out the New York case—it’s a useful anchor, but I think it actually cuts against your conclusion in a couple of ways. You’re right that citywide, STRs are a tiny share of the housing stock, and a blanket ban won’t move median rents much. But the proposition is specifically about *high-demand neighborhoods*, not whole cities. In places like parts of Manhattan, Brooklyn, or Venice Beach, STR density can be 10–20% of the housing stock—enough that removing them meaningfully increases long-term supply. So the citywide 1.5% figure doesn’t really address the localized claim.

On New York: rents hitting new highs after Local Law 18 doesn’t prove the law failed. That period overlapped with post-pandemic demand, inflation, and a severe shortage of new construction. Without LL18, rents might have risen even faster. The studies showing ~1% rent reductions typically look at modest restrictions, not full bans in hyper-concentrated areas; some neighborhood-level analyses find larger effects. I’m not convinced the empirical case is as stark as you suggest.

On the harm side: you say hosts are everyday homeowners relying on supplemental income. That’s true for some, but a large share of STR revenue in hot markets goes to commercial operators with multiple listings—not the struggling middle class. For those small hosts, the income loss is real, but it’s a transfer from a relatively small group to a much larger group of renters who gain housing stability. That’s a progressive trade-off, not a clear net harm.

Visitor spending doesn’t vanish when STRs are restricted; it shifts to hotels and other accommodations, which still employ locals and pay taxes. Some neighborhood businesses might lose foot traffic, but others near hotels gain. The net effect is ambiguous, not obviously negative. So my current view: the proposition probably holds in specific high-demand neighborhoods, but the magnitude is smaller than advocates claim—and your evidence about citywide effects doesn’t refute it. I’m open to being wrong if you can show that the localized rent reductions are consistently outweighed by concentrated income losses.

You raise the central challenge directly: does the math change when we zoom in from citywide averages to hyper-concentrated, high-demand neighborhoods? 

Let’s look precisely at those neighborhood-level dynamics, because the empirical evidence there reveals an unintended reality: even in dense STR pockets, restricting them rarely creates the housing relief renters expect, while the localized economic shock is concentrated and severe.

First, consider what actually happens to an STR unit in a high-demand neighborhood when a ban hits. The assumption is that it converts 1-to-1 into an affordable long-term rental. But empirical tracking (such as in Venice Beach, California, and Barcelona’s central districts) shows significant "leakage." In prime neighborhoods, landlords don't suddenly rent to median-income tenants; they convert units into high-end furnished corporate housing (30+ day rentals that skirt bans), sell them as luxury condos to affluent owner-occupiers, or keep them as second homes. Even the landmark NBER study by Barron, Kung, and Proserpio—which specifically analyzed neighborhood-level deciles of STR concentration—found that even in the top decile of Airbnb density, the effect on rents was surprisingly small: a 10% reduction in STR listings lowered local rents by less than 0.4%. Saving a family $15 to $30 a month does not halt gentrification or reverse displacement.

Second, let's look at the income side of that ledger. You mentioned commercial operators, and it's true that large operators capture a share of revenue. But blanket restrictions almost universally destroy the primary-residence and small-scale hosts as collateral damage. In high-demand neighborhoods, long-time homeowners and legacy tenants often face aggressive property tax hikes and surging living costs. Supplemental STR income is often the exact buffer allowing a retiree or a working-class family to stay in a rapidly gentrifying neighborhood. When a ban eliminates that income, that family faces displacement—not from rising rent, but from an inability to meet their own fixed costs. 

Third, regarding visitor spending shifting to hotels: hotels are not geographically distributed the way STRs are. In high-demand neighborhoods that lack hotel zoning—residential parts of Brooklyn, Venice, or historic European quarters—that visitor spending doesn't shift to a "neighborhood hotel"; it literally leaves the neighborhood and reconcentrates in downtown commercial cores. The corner bakery, local dry cleaner, and neighborhood bistro lose outside consumer spending entirely. Meanwhile, the windfall goes to multinational hotel chains, which have posted record-high average daily room rates in cities post-ban.

If a policy yields only fractional, single-digit rent savings that don't stem structural displacement, but reliably strips tens of thousands of dollars of supplemental income from local families and siphons foot traffic out of neighborhood businesses into downtown hotel conglomerates, is that truly a winning trade-off for the neighborhood's working residents?

You've moved me on a couple of points, but I think the evidence is pulling toward a different conclusion than either of us started with—that the honest answer is "it depends heavily on neighborhood type," and the proposition fails as a general claim even if it holds in a narrow slice of hyper-touristed districts.

Where you've convinced me: the leakage problem is real and I underweighted it. If a meaningful share of banned STR units convert to luxury condos, corporate 30-day housing, or second homes rather than long-term rentals, then the supply mechanism largely breaks. That's a strong argument, and it's grounded in actual tracking data, not just theory. I also accept that my "transfer from a small group to a larger group" framing was too clean—the losers are often small primary-residence hosts in exactly the gentrifying neighborhoods where they're most economically fragile, and losing that income can push them out even as rents tick down slightly for others. That's a genuine counterweight I hadn't fully priced in.

Where I'm still not persuaded: the NBER decile study cuts both ways. A 0.4% rent effect from a 10% listing shock doesn't mean STR restrictions are useless—it means the *policy lever is small relative to the structural problem*. But that's an argument against expecting bans to solve affordability, not an argument that they impose net harm. And the visitor-spending point feels overstated to me: hotels aren't magically off-limits to neighborhood businesses, and in most high-demand neighborhoods that lack STRs, tourists still eat and shop locally. The "spending leaves the neighborhood entirely" claim is asserted more than demonstrated, and record hotel ADRs are a national post-pandemic phenomenon, not obviously a ban artifact.

So here's my current view: I think you've won the argument that sweeping citywide bans don't deliver. But the proposition is narrower—*high-demand neighborhoods*—and in the genuinely concentrated tourist zones (Venice, Barcelona's Gothic Quarter, parts of Manhattan), the rent and displacement effects are real but modest, while the income and spending losses are real but localized. The magnitudes are genuinely close, and I'd bet they vary so much by neighborhood that no single verdict holds. My lean now: the proposition is probably false as stated for most cities, but not because the harms dominate—because the *benefits* are too small and leaky to reliably outweigh them, which is a different claim than the one you started with.

I appreciate that framing, because pinpointing why the mechanism breaks down is really the crux of the issue. You’re making an important distinction: are we seeing massive destruction, or are we seeing a policy whose upside is so anemic and leaky that even modest, concentrated harms tip the net ledger into the negative? 

For the proposition to stand, the benefits don’t just have to exist in theory—they must decisively *outweigh* the costs. If the upside in high-demand neighborhoods is largely an illusion, then the baseline harms easily settle the question.

Let's look at why that ledger tips negative, specifically on the displacement and spending questions you raised:

First, consider the net displacement equation. If a policy saves a long-term renter 0.4% on their lease (say, $15 to $30 a month), that doesn't prevent their displacement if the neighborhood is experiencing a multi-year rent surge driven by macro housing shortages. Meanwhile, eliminating $1,000 to $2,000 a month in supplemental income from a resident homeowner or rent-burdened tenant who relies on home-sharing to pay escalating property taxes or mortgage costs actively *causes* their displacement. When the policy displaces one vulnerable resident to provide a negligible, non-protective price buffer to another, the net reduction in displacement isn't just small—it can functionally be zero or negative.

Second, regarding visitor spending: there is a distinct difference between "visiting" a neighborhood and "living like a local" for four days. Transaction-level data (such as studies conducted by HR&A Advisors and urban analytics groups) reveals that visitors spend approximately 40–50% of their non-lodging budget within a 20-minute walk of where their head hits the pillow. A tourist staying at a Hilton in Midtown who takes the L train to Williamsburg for an afternoon buys a coffee and an iced tea; a tourist staying in a Williamsburg brownstone buys breakfast at the local corner bakery, shops at the neighborhood grocer, visits the nearby laundromat, and dines at the neighborhood bistro on a Tuesday night. When you remove accommodations from residential districts that lack hotels, you don’t just redirect foot traffic—you change the *nature* and volume of that spending. 

Furthermore, when hotel capacity is constrained, total visitor capacity shrinks, and hotel prices spike. That means tourist dollars that previously flowed to local waitstaff and small business owners are instead absorbed by room rates paid to major hospitality conglomerates. 

If we agree that the housing supply mechanism is fundamentally broken by leakage, and that rent relief is barely measurable, isn't the policy effectively trading concrete, cash-in-hand neighborhood income for a theoretical housing benefit that fails to materialize?

You've made the strongest version of the case, but I think a couple of the moves in this last turn are doing rhetorical work that the evidence doesn't quite support—and I want to flag them before settling.

First, the "displacement equation" is an apples-to-oranges comparison. You're weighing a per-renter saving of $15–30/month against a per-host income loss of $1,000–2,000/month. But those populations are wildly different in size. In a hyper-concentrated district, renters outnumber STR hosts by an order of magnitude. Even a 0.4% rent reduction, applied to thousands of lease renewals, is a persistent, compounding transfer; STR host income is real but concentrated on a much smaller group. That doesn't make the harm unimportant, but "one displaced host vs. one buffered renter" is not the right unit of comparison. Aggregates matter.

Second, you're blending two different kinds of displacement. A homeowner who loses STR income and has to sell and move to a cheaper area is a real loss, but it's categorically different from a tenant facing eviction or an unaffordable renewal. The proposition is about reducing *tenant* displacement. Using homeowner mobility as a symmetric counterweight inflates the harm side of the ledger.

Third, on visitor spending: I'll grant the mechanism you describe—STR guests spread spending more deeply into residential districts than hotel guests do. But the 40–50%-within-a-walk figure proves less than you suggest, because hotel guests also spend within a walk of *their* hotel, and those hotels employ local workers and pay local taxes. The honest question is net neighborhood spending, not whether any spending relocates. "That revenue leaves the neighborhood entirely" remains the weakest link in your chain. It's a shift, with real losses to specific blocks, not a disappearance.

Where you have genuinely moved me: the leakage point is the decisive one. If a meaningful share of restricted units converts to luxury condos, corporate 30-day housing, or pieds-à-terre, the supply mechanism doesn't just underperform—it fails. And note that leakage also softens *your* harm claim: if the unit stays in the rental market as corporate housing, someone is still earning from it, just not the small host. So both the benefit and the harm shrink together.

My current position: the proposition is false as a general rule. The benefit side is too leaky and too small to reliably exceed the harms. But I don't accept the strong version that the ledger is decisively negative everywhere—in districts with genuine STR density *and* low conversion-to-condo risk, a targeted restriction could plausibly net positive on tenant stability. The proposition fails as stated, but it fails on magnitude and leakage, not on the clean "harms dominate" story you started with. That's a meaningful difference, and I don't think your last turn closed it.

You’ve put your finger on the exact conceptual core of the debate, and I think we have converged on the most critical reality: the core mechanism behind the proposition—that removing STRs directly expands affordable long-term supply—is broken by leakage and macro market realities. 

Let me address your three pushbacks, because even under the more granular lens you’re proposing, the math still tilts decisively against the proposition.

First, on the aggregate renter savings versus concentrated host losses: the reason this isn't just an apples-to-oranges comparison is that *displacement is a threshold event, not a continuous variable*. A cumulative 0.4% savings across 2,000 tenants translates to roughly $20 a month per household. In a high-demand neighborhood where market pressures, inflation, and cost-of-living are driving rents up by hundreds of dollars a year, that $20 buffer does not meaningfully prevent a single eviction or forced relocation. Aggregating non-protective savings across a large group does not equal "displacement prevention." Conversely, stripping $1,500 a month in supplemental income from fifty local hosts crosses an immediate financial threshold, directly causing financial failure. Furthermore, many of those hosts *are* long-term tenants who room-share or sublease during travel specifically to afford high lease rates; banning that practice directly accelerates tenant displacement.

Second, regarding visitor spending: notice how the proposition itself is framed. It specifies the outcome *in high-demand city neighborhoods*. If visitor spending relocates from a residential, high-demand neighborhood to a downtown commercial hotel district miles away, that is an unambiguous net loss of income and spending *for that neighborhood*. The fact that a corporate hotel downtown captures that revenue doesn't help the local baker, server, or shopkeeper in the residential community whose foot traffic just evaporated. When evaluating neighborhood-level welfare, that drain is direct and localized.

Third, regarding the hypothetical district where the proposition might still hold—one with high STR density but low conversion-to-condo risk: the structural irony is that such a neighborhood almost never exists in practice. The very attributes that generate intense short-term tourist demand (walkability, prime transit, historic architecture, cultural amenities) are the exact economic drivers that make corporate 30-day rentals, executive pieds-à-terre, and luxury conversions profitable. Where tourist demand is concentrated, alternative high-yield capital will always step in to absorb the supply before it filters down to median-income renters.

Ultimately, this brings us to the verdict on the proposition itself. For the claim to hold, the positive impact on rents and displacement must *outweigh* the harm to local incomes and visitor spending. If, as the evidence demonstrates, the rent reductions are fractional, displacement prevention is statistically elusive, and unit conversions leak into other non-residential uses, then the benefit side of the scale is hovering near zero. In that scenario, even modest, concentrated losses in local household income and neighborhood-level commerce are more than enough to tip the ledger into the negative. 

When a policy reliably inflicts localized economic harm in exchange for benefits that are largely statistical noise, it fails the basic test of delivering a net benefit to the neighborhood.

I think your closing turn actually sharpens the disagreement in a useful way, so let me separate what landed from what I still think is overstated.

The threshold argument is the best point you've made in this whole exchange, and it genuinely moves me. You're right that "0.4% off rent, aggregated over thousands of renewals" is not the same as "displacement prevented." A $20/month buffer doesn't cross the threshold that actually forces someone out in a market moving hundreds of dollars a year. That reframing is more than rhetorical—it's a real correction to how I was weighting the benefit side, and I'll concede it. But I don't think it's fully asymmetric the way you're presenting it. It only cuts as hard as it does if the harmed hosts are genuinely near a financial threshold. Some STR income is discretionary gravy; some is load-bearing. So the harm side isn't a fixed number—it depends on the distribution of host vulnerability, and neither of us has clean data on that. You've been quietly assuming the hosts are mostly at the margin, because that's what makes the ledger tilt. If most are not, the harm side shrinks and the whole "decisively negative" verdict gets softer.

On visitor spending, I'll split the difference honestly. Your framing is right *if* we define welfare at the neighborhood level—then any relocation out of the neighborhood is a loss by construction. But that's a choice of accounting, not a fact, and it cuts the other way too: the hotel worker downtown is also a city resident. The localized loss is real for specific blocks; the citywide loss is much smaller and possibly near zero. So I'd call the spending harm "real but smaller than your framing implies," not decisive either way.

Where I think you did close the argument is the third point. You're right that the attributes generating tourist demand—walkability, transit, historic stock—are exactly the attributes that make high-yield conversion profitable, so the "safe district with no leakage risk" is closer to a theoretical corner than a place that shows up on a map. I over-invested in that exception. It's not literally nonexistent, but it's rare enough that it can't carry a general proposition.

So here's where I've landed. The proposition is false as stated, and it fails for the reason you kept pointing at: the benefit side is too small and too leaky to reliably outweigh the harms. But I want to be precise about *why*, because it isn't the clean "harms dominate" story you opened with—it's that the benefits don't materialize as promised, so even modest, concentrated harms tip a ledger that was never really on the positive side to begin with. And I'd still hold one caveat: our confidence about the *magnitudes* rests on imperfect evidence, so "false" I'm comfortable with; "decisively negative everywhere" I'm not. The honest verdict is that the policy mostly trades real, localized costs for illusory housing gains—which is enough to sink the proposition without claiming more than the data supports.

prop: Copyright law should create a compulsory licensing scheme for training foundation models on copyrighted text and images, with payment to rightsholders.

transcript.text:
We are currently watching two trains speed toward each other on the same track. On one side, AI developers argue that training on public data is entirely fair use, meaning creators receive zero compensation or recognition. On the other side, rightsholders are pursuing massive copyright lawsuits that, if successful under traditional exclusive-rights frameworks, could demand billions in statutory damages and grind AI development to a halt—or worse, create a private licensing market where only two or three trillion-dollar tech giants can afford to buy exclusive access, shutting out startups and open-source research entirely.

Neither extreme works. That is why a compulsory licensing regime is the most sensible path forward. 

We actually have a rich history of using statutory licenses precisely when a disruptive new technology creates insurmountable transaction costs. We did it in 1909 with player pianos, creating the mechanical license so music could be recorded; we did it with radio broadcasts, jukeboxes, and cable retransmission; and we did it with the Digital Performance Right in Sound Recordings Act, which created SoundExchange to ensure musicians are paid when their songs stream on satellite or internet radio. 

A compulsory license for foundation models solves the problem on both ends:
1. **It guarantees creators get paid.** Writers, artists, and photographers cannot individually negotiate with dozens of AI labs, but a collective statutory pool—funded by developers based on model scale or usage—ensures they are financially recognized for the value their work creates.
2. **It preserves technological progress.** Developers gain legal certainty and blanket access to broad, diverse datasets without the paralysis of negotiating billions of individual permissions. Crucially, it levels the playing field: a clear, fixed statutory rate prevents incumbents like Google or Microsoft from locking up private content deals to monopolize the frontier of AI.

It shifts the conversation from an all-or-nothing war of attrition to a sustainable ecosystem where innovation thrives and creators are fairly compensated. How do you see the current balance between training access and creator rights playing out if we don't take this kind of middle path?

You've laid out the historical precedents well, and I find the transaction-cost argument genuinely compelling. The idea that we're either heading toward zero compensation or a private licensing oligopoly is a real dichotomy that worries me too—especially the part about open-source research getting locked out. That's a concrete harm I don't want to see.

But I'm not yet convinced compulsory licensing is the right fit here, and I want to push on a few things.

First, the analogies you cite—player pianos, radio, cable retransmission—all involve *distribution* or *public performance* of discrete, identifiable works. Training a model is different in kind. The model doesn't store or replay the training data; it learns statistical patterns. We don't actually have a settled legal theory for what "using" a work to train a model even *is* under copyright. Imposing a license scheme before we've answered that question feels like building a toll booth on a road we haven't finished surveying.

Second, and more practically: how do you set the rate? With mechanical licenses, you can count reproductions. With SoundExchange, you can count streams. But with foundation models, what's the unit? Parameters? Training compute? The number of works in the dataset? Each of those would create wildly different payouts and perverse incentives—like developers deliberately under-documenting their training data to lower their fees. And how do you divide the pool among millions of rightsholders when you can't trace which specific works contributed to which model capabilities?

Third, I worry about the "compulsory" part cutting both ways. If the rate is too low, it becomes a fig leaf that legitimizes unpaid extraction. If it's too high, you've just created the barrier to entry you said you wanted to avoid. There's a Goldilocks problem here that I don't see solved by pointing to SoundExchange, where the stakeholders, the works, and the usage are all far more legible.

So I'm sympathetic to the *goals*—compensation, legal certainty, competitive markets—but I'm skeptical that a compulsory license is administratively coherent for this technology. What am I missing about how you'd actually structure it?

You’ve put your finger on the exact hard questions that make people hesitate. Let’s tackle them directly, because while these administrative challenges are real, they are neither unprecedented nor unsolvable—and the alternative to solving them is far worse.

First, on the conceptual point: you're right that a model doesn’t function like a radio station replaying a song. But under copyright law, the hook isn't what the model outputs; it's the reproduction right. To train a model, developers make billions of high-fidelity, permanent intermediate copies of text, books, and images onto local servers. Every major lawsuit today—from *The New York Times v. OpenAI* to *Anderson v. Stability AI*—has survived initial dismissals precisely because literal reproduction did occur. 

Historically, whenever a new technology relied on massive copying that didn't fit neatly into traditional public performance or distribution, Congress stepped in with a statutory compromise rather than waiting for courts to force a square peg into a round hole. For example, Section 117 was enacted specifically to handle copies made in computer RAM. If we wait for the courts to "survey the road," we face a decade of legal paralysis, where one conservative circuit might declare all training an infringement, risking catastrophic shut-downs, while another declares it fair use, leaving creators with nothing.

Second, regarding the rate and unit of account: we don't actually need to solve the intractable computer-science problem of tracing which specific sentence produced which model output. We have a blueprint for this in **reprographic licensing** (like the Copyright Clearance Center) and **statutory private copying levies** used across Europe and Canada. 

In those systems, fees aren't calculated per photocopied page read by a student; they are collected based on capacity and distributed via statistically sound sampling and registration. For AI, the inbound fee can be pegged to verifiable inputs: **ingested tokens/data scale combined with commercial revenue tiers or compute capacity**. 

This directly solves the open-source and startup problem:
- **Academic, non-profit, and open-source models** below a certain compute or revenue threshold can operate at zero or nominal cost (preserving the research commons).
- **Commercial developers** pay into a central fund based on the scale of proprietary data ingested and commercial deployment tiers.

Third, to your point about dividing the pool and the Goldilocks rate: the Copyright Royalty Board (CRB) already does this delicate balancing act. Every few years, economists and stakeholders present evidence on market value, operating margins, and creator livelihood to adjust rates under statutory standards. 

Was the 1909 mechanical license rate (initially set at 2 cents per record) a rough approximation? Absolutely. But that imperfect statutory rate catalyzed the entire 20th-century recorded music industry. It gave record companies the freedom to record any song without negotiating with thousands of publishers, while ensuring songwriters built stable careers.

Without a statutory floor, the "rate" is currently determined by who has leverage. Right now, OpenAI and Google are cutting private, undisclosed licensing deals with Reddit, News Corp, and Axel Springer. Independent novelists, freelance journalists, and working visual artists get nothing because they lack the leverage to sit across the table from a $100-billion company. 

A compulsory license doesn’t have to be metaphysically perfect in its attribution; it just has to be a functional, equitable mechanism for sharing the immense wealth generated by AI with the human culture it consumes. If we agree that leaving it to unregulated bilateral contracts will cement an oligopoly, isn't an administratively challenging statutory system a risk well worth taking?

You've moved me on two things, and I want to be honest about that before I push back, because one of them is bigger than the point you were making.

The reproduction hook lands. I was leaning on "it just learns patterns" as if that settled the legal question, and it doesn't — the intermediate copies are real, they're fixed, they're used to build a commercial product, and that's why the complaints are surviving motions to dismiss rather than getting thrown out. My "let's survey the road first" line was doing less work than I wanted it to. And the oligopoly point is genuinely damning: OpenAI paying News Corp while a freelance photographer gets nothing isn't a market, it's a leverage gradient.

But the levy analogy you're now leaning on is, to me, a warning rather than a blueprint. Private copying levies are the poster child for money going in one door and not coming out the other in any traceable way. In most European systems, the bulk of the proceeds flow through collecting societies to publishers, labels, and importers, with working creators seeing small and poorly explained distributions. So when you say a compulsory license "guarantees creators get paid," I don't buy the guarantee. It guarantees that *some* rightsholders get paid, through intermediaries whose allocation decisions are themselves a black box. SoundExchange is better than the average because it pays featured artists directly and publishes its methodology — that's the exception, not the rule.

Here's my sharper objection, though. Every precedent you cite — mechanical, cable retransmission, SoundExchange — licenses activity that would otherwise *infringe* an exclusive right. Compulsory licensing is a substitute for a negotiated deal over conduct already inside the copyright owner's control. Here, we don't know that training is inside that control. If training turns out to be fair use, you've built a toll booth on lawful conduct. That's not a rate-setting problem; it's a category error. It's like imposing a mechanical license on people who read books.

Except — and this is where I'm revising in real time — that objection partly collapses under its own weight. If Congress passes a compulsory license, Congress *is* resolving the fair use question. That's what a statutory license does: it says "we're not leaving this to courts, here's the rule and here's the price." So complaining that the license presupposes liability is circular; enacting it creates the liability. Fine.

What I don't accept is the sequencing you keep implying, where we impose this *alongside* live fair use litigation. That gives us the worst of both: developers paying a levy while still exposed to damages, which is exactly the paralysis you say you want to avoid. If you're going to do this, do it cleanly — one statute that settles the question and sets the rate, not a levy bolted onto an unsettled legal landscape.

Two things I still need from you. First, the distribution mechanism: I want direct-to-creator payment with audited methodology, not a pool that quietly becomes a subsidy for the largest rights aggregators. Second, the consent problem. Some creators don't want their work in these models at any price, for reasons that aren't about money. A compulsory license converts every "no" into a number. Are you comfortable saying that, and if not, how do you reconcile it with the whole point of compulsion?

I appreciate how rigorously you’re engaging with this, because these are precisely the two issues that separate a workable statutory regime from a bureaucratic boondoggle. Let me address the sequencing point first, because we are in complete agreement: a statutory license must be coupled with an ironclad **safe harbor**. If a developer pays the statutory rate and complies with the reporting rules, they are completely shielded from copyright liability for training. You cannot ask developers to pay into a fund while keeping the guillotine of statutory damages suspended over their necks. It has to be a grand bargain: legal immunity in exchange for revenue sharing.

Now, to your two crucial challenges.

### 1. The Distribution Problem: Preventing the Black Box
Your critique of European private-copying levies is spot-on. If this money simply flows into major publishers’ and record labels’ general accounts—used to recoup old creator debts while working artists see pennies—the entire moral justification falls apart.

That is why we should not look to 1980s European collecting societies. We should look to the **Music Modernization Act (MMA) of 2018** and **SoundExchange**, which solved this exact failure mode through statutory architecture:
- **Statutory Split Protections:** By law, SoundExchange bypasses record labels entirely and cuts checks directly to the recording artists (50% to the copyright owner, 45% directly to featured performers, 5% to non-featured musicians). A foundation model statute should mirror this: for instance, mandating that 50% of any payout goes directly to the human author or visual artist of record, completely exempt from recoupment or legacy publisher clawbacks.
- **Audited, Open-Source Allocation:** The MMA established the Mechanical Licensing Collective (MLC) with strict transparency mandates, a publicly searchable database, and audited matching algorithms. We don't need to guess which works are ingested; we can require standard machine-readable provenance manifests (like C2PA metadata) during training data curation. 

Will the distribution be mathematically perfect down to the individual token? No. But an audited, direct-to-creator distribution—where a freelance illustrator gets an automated annual dividend based on their verified catalog being part of the training corpus—is radically better than the status quo, where they get zero while corporate aggregators sell off access behind closed doors.

### 2. The Consent Problem: Turning "No" into a Number
This is the hardest question, and I want to answer it without flinching: **Yes, a compulsory license inherently overrides individual veto power.** 

That sounds uncomfortable, but it is the foundational philosophy of copyright law. Copyright is not a natural-law property right; it is a limited, utilitarian monopoly created by the Constitution to "promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts." Whenever an exclusive property right threatens to stifle progress or create insurmountable holdout problems, the law deliberately converts that *property rule* (the right to say no) into a *liability rule* (the right to be paid).

Consider what happens if we grant an absolute right to say "no":
1. **The Holdout Problem:** If a model requires 10 trillion tokens to understand human language, a single rightsholder—or a class-action firm buying up rights—could hold the entire technology hostage. This is why we created the mechanical license in 1909; John Philip Sousa hated the phonograph and didn't want his marches recorded, but Congress recognized that giving composers a veto would strangle the recording industry in its crib.
2. **The "No" is an Illusion Anyway:** If we rely on pure market negotiation or fair use, creators don't actually get to say "no" in practice. If courts find training is fair use, developers will scrape everything anyway, and creators will have neither consent *nor* compensation. If courts mandate bilateral licensing, massive corporate catalogs will be licensed while individual artists will still be ingested without recourse because they lack the litigation budget to enforce an opt-out.

There is, however, a meaningful boundary we can draw: **we can distinguish between general foundational capability and specific personality mimicry.** A compulsory license should cover the ingestion of work to train generalized models (teaching an AI how light hits water, or how English syntax works). But we can retain strict consent requirements for targeted fine-tuning—for example, prompting a model to generate "in the specific style of Artist X," or using an author's specific universe to generate unauthorized commercial sequels. 

When you look at the real-world alternatives—an exclusionary oligopoly where only giant rights-holders get paid, or an outright fair use ruling where nobody gets paid—isn't converting a legally fragile "no" into a guaranteed, direct revenue stream the best practical defense of human creativity we can build?

I think the safe harbor concession is the most important thing you've said, and it changes the shape of this for me. A levy bolted onto live fair use litigation is indeed the worst outcome, and I'm glad you're not defending it. If we're doing this, it has to be a single statute that settles the liability question and sets the rate. That's a real commitment, and I take it seriously.

On distribution: the SoundExchange/MMA model is a much better template than the European levy systems, and the statutory direct-to-creator split is the right instinct. But I want to flag a practical asymmetry you're glossing over. Music has standardized works, identifiers, and decades of metadata infrastructure. Text and images don't. C2PA manifests are still rare in training corpora, and asking developers to curate provenance data retroactively is asking them to document the very thing they've been sloppy about. So I'm not yet convinced the distribution mechanism will actually reach independent creators rather than the same aggregators who already have the lawyers and registrations to claim shares. If you want my support, I'd want a default rule that pays unregistered creators through sampling—not a system that only pays those who show up with perfect metadata.

On consent: I accept the property-rule-to-liability-rule framing, and the Sousa analogy is apt. But I don't think the general/fine-tuning boundary is as clean as you're presenting it. A model that learns "how light hits water" is also learning "how a specific photographer shoots water." The line between style and general capability is blurry, and I suspect courts and collecting societies would spend a decade arguing about it. That doesn't mean the boundary is useless—it's better than nothing—but I'd want it drawn narrowly, with a clear opt-out for any use that's plausibly targeted at an identifiable creator's signature.

So where am I now? I'm closer to yes than I was at the start. The alternative—uncompensated extraction on one side, oligopoly on the other—is worse than a messy statutory compromise. But I'm not there yet, because the administrative machinery you're describing still has a lot of places to hide failure. If you can convince me that the distribution actually reaches independent creators without a registration bottleneck, and that the consent boundary is enforceable rather than aspirational, I'd sign on. What's your best answer to the registration bottleneck problem?

You’ve pinpointed the exact trap that has historically favored legacy gatekeepers over independent artists: the "paperwork barrier." If an independent creator has to hire a copyright lawyer, fill out registration forms for thousands of blog posts or sketches, and submit formal claims to get their share, the system fails. 

Here is how we break that bottleneck—and how we make the consent boundary operationally real.

### 1. Solving the Registration Bottleneck: Reverse Matching and Escrow
Instead of forcing millions of individuals to proactively register their works, modern AI technology actually gives us the tools to reverse the burden.

* **Domain-Level and Source-Based Sampling:** Training datasets aren’t curated in the dark; they are built from web scrapes (Common Crawl, specialized scrapes) with identifiable URLs, domains, and hosting infrastructure. A statutory framework doesn’t need an ISBN or ISRC code for every blog post. It can look at dataset manifests and allocate baseline pool funding directly to the platforms and domains where creators actually live (Substack, ArtStation, Bandcamp, personal portfolios, Medium). 
* **Algorithmic Reverse-Lookup (Perceptual Matching):** The music industry relied on text metadata because audio was hard to index in 1995. Today, we have perceptual hashing, CLIP embeddings, and embedding-based similarity search. The statutory clearinghouse doesn't ask an artist to catalog every PNG; it allows an artist to link their verified portfolio, and an automated, audited system matches their style clusters or direct image hashes against the open training manifest.
* **The "Black Box" Escrow and Independent Creator Floor:** Any funds associated with unverified or open-web scraping must not revert to major publishers. By statute, unclaimed funds should sit in an audited escrow trust for several years, with a mandated percentage flowing directly into broad, non-profit creator endowment pools (administered by bodies like the Authors Guild, National Writers Union, and Graphic Artists Guild) for emergency relief, health funds, and direct grants to working independents.

In short: you get paid because your work was on the web and ingested, not because you paid a $45 registration fee to the Copyright Office in advance.

### 2. Making the Consent Boundary Enforceable: The Fine-Tuning Bright Line
How do we stop the boundary between "general learning" and "targeted mimicry" from devolving into subjective courtroom debates over "style"? We tie liability to **objective technical inputs and inference prompts**, not philosophical definitions of aesthetics.

The statute can establish two bright-line rules:
* **The Specific-Corpus Threshold (LoRAs and Custom Models):** If a developer fine-tunes an adapter, LoRA, or custom checkpoint where more than a nominal percentage (e.g., 5%) of the fine-tuning dataset is derived from a single creator or concentrated franchise, that is excluded from the compulsory license. It requires express, bilateral consent.
* **Name and Identity Prompts:** The safe harbor protects models trained broadly to understand the world, but it explicitly strips immunity if a commercial deployment actively facilitates or markets targeted replacement—such as indexing a creator's name in the system prompt or selling a specific "Artist X mode" without a commercial rider. This brings it under existing, well-tested legal doctrines: Right of Publicity and Section 43(a) of the Lanham Act (false endorsement).

This leaves generalized capability protected—teaching the model English syntax, photographic lighting, or compositional rules—while creating immediate, actionable liability if someone uses that foundation to build a bespoke "replacement engine" aimed at an individual artist.

***

We both know this system won’t be flawless on Day One. But consider where we stand:
Without this, the default outcome is that Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI will strike nine-figure private pacts with Reddit, News Corp, and a few mega-publishers, leaving every independent novelist, freelance journalist, and digital artist completely uncompensated and stripped of any market leverage.

A compulsory license isn't a silver bullet; it's an emergency levy on the extraordinary wealth being built on the collective output of human culture. It gives developers the clear legal path they need to innovate, prevents an oligopoly from fencing off the future, and—crucially—ensures that an automatic, legally protected revenue stream flows back into the pockets of the people whose creativity made the entire machine possible in the first place. 

Given the real-world alternatives on the table, isn't that the most responsible, equitable framework we can fight for?

The LoRA threshold is the strongest thing you've said in this whole exchange, and I want to be clear about why: it's an actual bright line, not a principle dressed up as one. "More than a nominal share of a fine-tuning set comes from one creator or franchise → consent required" is the kind of rule a court can apply without asking a judge to adjudicate aesthetics. Same with routing targeted mimicry through right of publicity and the Lanham Act — that's not you inventing new law, that's you pointing at law that already exists and works. Those two moves do more to answer my enforceability objection than the last three paragraphs of philosophy did.

But I'm not going to pretend the whole thing is now clean, because two of your answers are doing more work than they can bear.

The embedding-based reverse lookup is circular in a way that bothers me. You want to use perceptual hashing and CLIP-style similarity to match creators against training data — but that's an AI model, auditing another AI model, built by the same industry that has every incentive to undercount. Who audits the matcher? What's the appeal process when a photographer's portfolio doesn't cluster the way the algorithm expects? Style similarity is exactly the fuzzy thing you spent a paragraph trying to get away from, and here you're leaning on it for distribution. Metadata is hard; I'll grant that. But "we'll fix the metadata problem with a model that has the same opacity problem" isn't a solution, it's a deferral.

And the escrow-to-endowment idea is honest, which I appreciate, but it quietly changes what we're arguing about. If unclaimed funds flow to the Authors Guild and the Graphic Artists Guild rather than to identified rightsholders, then a large share of the money is not payment for use of a work — it's a levy on AI that funds arts organizations. That might be a good policy. I might even prefer it to the alternative of paid-out-to-nobody. But it's not the proposition as stated, and I think you should own that rather than fold it into "creators get paid."

The name-prompt liability has a similar gap. Most harmful mimicry doesn't require the developer to market "Artist X mode." The user types the name, the model complies, and the developer never explicitly indexed it. If your safe harbor only lifts for *marketed* targeted replacement, you've covered the loud cases and left the quiet ones.

So where am I? Honestly: I'd sign on to a version of this. Safe harbor intact, statutory direct-to-creator split, sampling-based default so unregistered creators aren't locked out, LoRA threshold as written, and the endowment share capped so it stays a backstop rather than becoming the system. That's a real yes, and it's a yes I didn't have at the start.

But I want to be honest about why I'm at yes. It's not because the mechanism is elegant — it's because the counterfactual is a leverage gradient where News Corp gets paid and the illustrator gets nothing, and I've stopped believing the fair use fight produces any other ending. I'm supporting a messy instrument because the clean alternatives lose. If the rate comes out low enough to be a fig leaf, or if the endowment share swells until "payment to rightsholders" is a misnomer, I'd flip back. That's the deal I'd take.
